review: Credit where it's due, the battle system is interesting mechanically and conceptually, and the game does provide some strategic advice, ultimately the outcome is based mostly on your level relative to your opponent. In a textbook example of a excessive difficulty spike, you can't progress without beating an opponent that'll likely be about twice your level, basically forcing you into a particularly slow level grind. I also found the tone and story concept to not jell that well.

Honestly. I love this game- to the point that a part of me wants to sit down and make a review video about this, because while it certainly is built on a funny concept - the execution is surprisingly thoughtful, and there is the start of some legitimately interesting worldbuilding, which makes it a shame that it's failed to see a sequel in a decade.

It also brings a rather interesting combat system to the table, which is neat enough to explore (though, it does reach its limits near the tail end of the game, especially since, while you will be making modular builds early on- it eventually becomes a matter of having *everything* - which removes some of the strategy the early game is built around).

Still, quite nifty- and definitely warrants checking out.

I bought this game years ago, played it, enjoyed it, then forgot about it. I came back to it for the first time in almost ten years yesterday, and honestly I think it's incredible.

In terms of technicality, it does show its age a little bit. There are very few settings (including no ability to change resolution), and no ability to skip the credits. I really don't think that's enough to ruin the experience for anyone, but maybe some people are more particular about that stuff.

But gameplay and story-wise, this absolutely holds up. The 'combat' system is incredibly tactical for having very few options and very little skill progression, but what few skills there are can make a surprising amount of difference in the course of a battle. (For example, consider whether equipping Firm Handshake will allow you to start the battle on a more strategically advantageous peg).

It's a steal at its full price, and even more of a steal on sale. The game can be beaten in about 4 hours if you know what you're doing, with extra content and secret-searching adding an extra few hours. Definitely not a game that overstays its welcome, and every minute in the game is spent with very clear ideas as to what you should be doing at the moment.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

OVERALL 9/10
Only worth a replay to reread the well-written story or because you particularly like the game play.

GRAPHICS 9/10
Simple, quasi-pixel RPG Maker fare that favours minimalism in regards to character design (characters are depicted as outlines filled in with their associated "house" colour). The environment is suitably cozy and the combat "animations" provide visual interest.

SOUND/MUSIC 9/10
Highly evocative soundtrack, excellent sounds effects and the minimalist-style humphs and scoffs of the voice actors immerse the player.

CONTROLS 8/10
My only sticking point is that it is possible to make a wrong decision when in combat due to the menu system not being intuitive (eg. the creator should put the category at the top of the subcategory menu [eg. Disruptive  - Subtle Common Overt, etc.] though that might qualify as a graphics / design issue).

PLOT 10/10
Powerful and moving well-written murder mystery style plot filled with twists and turns (THAT MAKE SENSE) that could stand toe-to-toe with a novel or a movie.  It's worth it to play (and replay) the game for the story alone! (Or go watch a playthrough >w>.)

GAMEPLAY 8/10
It has its moments. The combat system takes a little getting used to but it is fairly intuitive and strategic. Combat is "resource gathering" / Final Fantasy-style "Fight Run Magic". You have to be very careful while selecting your move for reasons mentioned earlier (sub-menus do not have the titles which should be there).

Grinding through conversations, investigating the environment and upgrading your character is intuitive, easy to do and fun!

FINAL VERDICT = "Murder mystery" style "This Game Is A Novel" with Final Fantasy style "Fight Run Magic" style resource-based "combat". Would recommend AT LEAST 1 playthrough.

The RPS is just a side thing that allows you to beat enemies at a lower level than you otherwise would. Outside of some optional combats for achievement purposes, the RPS system can be outright ignored for the entire duration of a playthough. The core of the combat is the resource management.
The game's combat mechanics are not anything crazy (either in difficulty or in originality), I can get why some people didn't *like* it, but why so many people outright failed to comprehend it is beyond me.

戦闘のシステムをざっと解説。
コマンドには三*三のフレーズの組み合わせがあり、
威圧Disruptive・懐柔Submissive・中傷Aggressive/婉曲subtle(弱)・通常common(中)・断言overt(強)
それぞれの組み合わせで三種の声色toneが決定される。「威圧*強=☆」など。

声色(○＞☆＞□＞○)はじゃんけんのように強さがあり、相手が前に出した手より強ければ、相手の精神防御が削れる。

まず威圧で「迫力power」を溜め、
次に懐柔でそのパワーを「機転tact」に変換し、
最後に中傷でタクトを消費して相手の心にダメージを与える。という流れ。

Last Word is a short game, but it also works well in terms of the content it packs into the experience.
The game is more of a mystery solving event as you try to find clues leading to an escape of sorts from your social obligations (much like myself in a party irl). 

Pros:
- The soundtrack is impeccable, each piece helps set a tone and you can really feel the emotion it's trying to convey (my personal favorite being the victory theme 'Fourth Appeal'.
- The combat system may well initially be of the rock, paper, scissors variety, but it has more to offer in terms of forward thinking in how to push your point without overexerting yourself, as well as occasionally planning for a slight loss for greater gain. The level system works well in presenting a slow increase in argumentative power, but with enough wit you can overturn a much more powerful opponent in discourse. Alternatively you could stomp laughably over those with much less power than yourself in a single move (Although understandably to avoid level grinding they'll stop arguing with you once they have no hope).
- Each character has a distinct feel to their personality and their interwoven reasons for attending help bring some more development to them.

Cons:
- Controls sometimes feel clunky, especially in terms of menu navigation and deciding on topics of interest. Controller support is also partial and doesn't work with some X-input devices.
- I did spend the first while wondering how to progress because the game never actually told me you could change your active topic or that you needed to in order to get new information.
- The ending leaves things somewhat ambiguous.

Overall I'd recommend it as an enjoyable, if short, experience. Although the soundtrack on its own feels worth it.

A game with a lot of charm! Play as Whitty Gawship, plucky photographer with a way for words. The cast of NPCs are a quirky assortment of nobility tropes that pose as informants and debate opponents. Gameplay is a mix of exploration, conversation, and verbal sparring. While in a debate, use a mixture of "attacks" to gather power and tact, and move the conversation forward to get the last word.
The script is cleverly written with genuine dialogue, fancy vocabulary, and witty puns. 
It is possible to grind levels to best harder opponents, but gameplay encourages using clever strategizing to squeak out a victory against tough foes.

This game is such a unique and enjoyable ride, played it on a sick day and kept me completely engaged and distracted from feeling crummy! 

The combat via discourse isn't just a gimmick--the designers put excellent thought into a combat system that requires planning, strategy, and tactics. Each option has different categories of tones, with each coming with various costs/benefits, and offering multiple ways to outsmart your opponent (or be outsmarted!). You can't just focus on 'scoring more', as your advantage isn't always based in points, but how you've set yourself up to affect and be affected. 

The story is okay--it's brief, but interwoven enough to warrant attention. There is a bit of mystery and sleuthing involved, and some actual benefits to paying attention (remembering what characters said, e.g.). The story does a good job of not giving itself away and setting up different pieces to join together. That said, I felt like the ending didn't make full use of all these pieces, and honestly it left me a bit disappointed. I felt like everything else was executed so well, so while it was OK, it just wasn't on par with the rest of the game. 

It's fun to play and the combat system is unique/challenging enough that I want to play again. I hope they make another game!

Last Word is an RPG-maker style game with discourse-based combat. In this setting, words have real power to change and control others' minds, as getting the titular "last word" in an argument leaves the other party susceptible to suggestion for a brief period of time.

As such, combat in this RPG is done not by swinging swords or shooting magic, but by carefully selecting from three types of phrase in three possible tones of voice in order to best your foe in an argument. There's a rock-paper-scissors style tactical component that can leave combatants more vulnerable to attack if the enemy capitalizes on their weakness, but each of the 9 attack types has their own advantages that make them worth considering even outside of that context. 

The art style is simple, but charming. With all of the characters colour-coded and drawn in a somewhat Edwardian style, this game really reminded me of Cluedo in its aesthetic appeal. Each character design is unique and decently caricatured, drawing your eye to their more outstanding features. It makes for a memorable experience. The various characters are also voiced in a somewhat unique style with mumble sounds in place of actual voiced dialogue. It's cute, and the range of different voices on display adds to the further characterization; however, it does leave me wondering how much stronger the theme might have come off with actual voiced dialogue. (As a plus, this probably made translation into other languages much cheaper.)

Between numerous colourful opponents and tactics you can learn, there's enough depth to sink your teeth into. Gameplay will appeal most to collectors and perfectionists, as there's a little bit of grind to unlock the content, as well as a fair bit of adventure game puzzle style "mash all the [dialogue phrases] on all of the available objects" between combat segments to learn the story, meet the characters, unlock progress, and find secrets.

As I definitely fall into that category, I really enjoyed Last Word, and I found a decent number of challenges available - especially in New Game+. The premise is novel enough to make me take a few hours from the latest hack-n-slash (in my case, Dead Cells) and enjoy uncovering a night of mystery and mayhem at a mysterious mansion. Marvelous.

A nice and rather compact game which has been made in RPGMaker, but don't let the shortness fool you as this is a very well executed concept. 

You, Whitty Gawship, have been invited by Professor Chatters to his estate for an evening engagement alongside a number of other Houses. By chatting with the other attendees you will learn about a variety of topics, which drive the plot without any information dumping.
The story telling is done well and interacting with the other characters also expands on the world you are in, the variety of wines you can find in the house is a lovely little way of world building and tying into the main story both subtly and neatly. This is world building done right, even the tutorial flows smoothly and builds upon the initial bare boned reason to be invited.

As with any rpg based game, you do have to fight you opponents and interact with the world to gain experience and level up. The mechanics for this a through a battle of wits, where who can get the last word in an engagement will win and be able to get the other person to do something you ask of them.
The 'combat' options are easy to grasp; it is based on the rock, paper, scissors format (though they are called something different where you have 3 discourse options and you have 3 options within each of these (which reflect the tone). The point is to balance these the build power and tact (which power your abilities and affect your opponents composure) to move the slider from its starting position to the challengers side of the bar - this represents you getting in the Last Word (beautifully tying into the name of the game!).  

The mechanics are very well balanced and it is easy to understand how player levels impact the starting point of the slider. The progression between levels is well paced and reasonable, plus you can use the bow ties you earn on levelling up and to buy the ability upgrades to boost your skills. 
I like how each character is colour coded, and this ties in with a topic of conversation which you can explore with the various guests at the party. It helps keep track of where you are in each topic and how much you have talked about it with each guest.

The story fits with the concept, though it could feel a little flimsy as you are only playing out one night - you are all gathered to learn about the Professor's latest invention, but he is not the most hospitable host and you need to figure out a way to meet him. I could easily see this as a tentative start to the creation a setting and the possibility of another game if the developers wanted.
The character names are rather clever, I do love the thought taken to relate them to synonyms for talking, to fit well to the theme of talking. The attention to detail is wonderful; it does make it easy to believe such a world is plausible and that the people living within it do have rivalries with each other and seek to get the last word in a conversation.

If you are looking for an entertaining game, with a dash of satire about upper class politics, to kill an afternoon this is one to pick up.

Short version: Last Word is a creative, clever little game, so long as you don't mind some repetitive moments. The occasional tedium of the battles is the price you'll pay for an interesting mystery with a series of interlocking secrets to unravel (and a truly inventive setting to boot).

Long version: At its core, Last Word a well-crafted adventure game with the addition of a conversation-themed RPG battle system. I say "conversation-themed" because no actual dialogue takes place - in pure mechanical terms, you're utilizing moves to raise certain resources, which you can then spend to move a marker into a goal zone.

If that sounds dry, it's because it is, but honestly, the system itself is cool! It has a rather elegant rock-paper-scissors aspect to it, and getting into the rhythm of its play can be exciting, especially once you learn abilities which trigger certain bonuses based on the marker's positioning. You actually have to pay attention and be strategic about your moves to win, which is nice.

But in order to progress the narrative, you have to grind at least a few levels in order to buy those abilities (and in order to start without a disadvantage when arguing with higher level characters). After awhile, that can't help but get tedious. If less grinding were involved, or if the arguments had a little more flavor/polish/visual interest, I have no doubt that no one would be complaining about this. But that's not the case, and so that has to be acknowledged.

All the same, Last Word's story is worth the relatively minor amount of repetitive gameplay involved. I love the way the characters' backstories interconnect. Figuring out who has the piece of information you need to unlock the next secret -- or where you can use the new information you just got -- is really fun. And the setting -- a world where getting the last word gives you literal power over others -- is unlike anything I've ever seen before. It's a fun game. It's a *different* game. I appreciate that more these days.

So, yeah. Come for the story, stay for the story (but honestly, the battle system isn't that bad -- just pick up the experience gain upgrade to save yourself some grinding).

Dwie rzeczy nie podobały mi się tu wyjątkowo: po pierwsze był to dziwaczny świat przedstawiony, w którym słowne przepychanki są na porządku dziennym, a jeśli się dyskurs wygra, to przeciwnik jest pokonany i zrobi wszystko, czego sobie życzymy. Dosłownie. Ciężko było mi wciągnąć się w walki poszczególnych domów szlacheckich, zrozumiec czemu właściwie służy wynalazek profesora, a głównej bohaterki - nieuprzejmej i uważającej się za nie wiadomo co - chyba nie da się polubić. Po drugie, system walki, który można z braku laku opisać jako papier, kamień, nożyce, po pewnym czasie stawał się bardzo męczący. A że gra czerpie z tradycji jRPG-ów, to niestety było trochę bezsensownego grindu. Tutaj właściwie aż się prosiło o dodanie dialogów, skoro to gra głównie o słowach. 

O wiele lepiej wypadła część, w której trzeba przeprowadzać dochodzenie i zbierać "plotki" od poszczeglnych osób, niemniej nie przykryło to niemiłego posmaku, który gra pozostawiła po sobie.

Mix between an adventure and an RPG game. You are trapped in a party with other guests, but there is no danger or pressing need to leave. You can't leave because the host asked you not to. So you have to solve a mystery to be able to convince him to let you go; otherwise it wouldn’t be polite to just leave. This compulsion to be polite is treated as some mystical force by the game, but otherwise that is pretty much it. So you have to gossip and chitchat with the other guests to gather clues, taste some wine, explore the (small) mansion, etc.
When you are trying to convince someone the game treats it like a battle, similarly to regular RPG battles. However, they require more strategy: you have 2 resources, a defense meter, and a struggle bar. Each move you make can generate resource A, transform resource A into resource B, or use one resource B to move the struggle bar. Your opponent tries to do the same thing, and the one that is able to move the struggle bar all the way into the other player side wins. Also, each move has an aspect that relates to the other moves in a rock-paper-scissors style; if you choose a move that beats the aspect of the last move made by the opponent, you hurt his defenses. This sounds pretty confusing, and at first it really is, but the game does a good job of showing you how it works. It's pretty fun for a while, but then the battles start dragging on. Going against strong opponents is always fun though.
Overall it's a good game that I can recommend.

This is a short and sweet RPG with unique and interesting "combat" mechanics that manages to densely pack a large amount of interesting, witty, enjoyable writing into a small area. While the game takes place entirely within a handful of rooms with a handful of characters, the game does a good job of packing every inch of the place with interesting things to inspect, and the characters are all filled with personality and interesting backgrounds to explore. The controls are somewhat odd for what I'm used to, both on keyboard and controller, and as far as I'm aware there's no in-game method to rebind the keys / buttons, but that is a small gripe for the sheer density of enjoyment in this game.

A single playthrough will probably take 3-5 hours, depending on how thoroughly you explore. There is a New Game+ function and a completion meter for those who want to see absolutely everything.

Although I was tempted to give this game a recommendation, I can't recommend this despite its unique gameplay and witty dialogue. If you are looking for a game filled with more adventure/action and immersive gameplay, I would suggest you look elsewhere. Last Word plays out like a narrative, but a relatively well-written one at that. 

Essentially, there are two main modes of gameplay: engaging in a "rock-paper-scissors" style combat and searching for clues to solve a secret word mystery. The battle system, although interesting at first, became quite tedious by the end of the game. There is very little variation in the different opponents you face and you'll end up repeating the same strategy over-and-over again to defeat them. On the other hand, I quite enjoyed the investigation sections. You're able to interact with objects and "discuss" different topics with characters in search of additional clues to progress the story. But once again, it became quite a tedious search trying to provide the correct clue to the right person. I sincerely liked the protagonist and all the other characters (plus, they all have the most amazing names) and it was fun to read what they all had to say. However, I felt that the restricted amount of gameplay really limited its potential. 

There's definitely a lot of good points about the game, but it isn't enough for me to give it a recommendation. Perhaps it is worth a purchase if on sale.
Finally, I can beat someone in an argument.

The worldbuilding is interesting too, building a universe that isn't *quite* our Earth.

Last Word is a mixture of Adventure and Role Playing games. It is a bit on the simple and grindy site, which can be make or break for the game. If you expect a dialogue heavy game with lots of options to chose from - this is not it.

Last Word puts you into a house party with an illustrious cast of characters that you will have to talk to on various occasions to advance the story and get some background information. Conversation is done by choosing one of nine key topics that will unlock bits of information you can then subsequently use in conversation with others or to interact with your surroundings. As such key topics basically act as items would in a Point&Click. To finish each chapter you will need to unlock a specific level of one topic and use it on the right character to start a discussion to "have the last word".

The combat system is basically a meter manager. You can build up your Power that has be converted into Tact that then can be used to move a peg on a scale towards the opponents end zone. Each action has three levels to it which will trade different amounts of resources, which adds a bit of tactic to the combat. Increase you power to the max or just a bit and additionally move the peg? Additionally each action has a certain tone to it which will influence your opponent. If you beat his tone in a rock, paper, scissor style you will make him lose countenance and make the peg move further.
There are some skills which will change the battles quite a bit like adding additional power if you land on certain fields or gaining Tact when matching the opponents tone. Which means the battles will get progressively more challenging.

While fighting these battles you will earn experience and every now and then get new Bows. The former also acts as a currency which you can purchase skills and new topics with, the later are loadout points which determine how many skills you can use at once.

Sadly the battle system is one of the big flaws. To beat the final fight of a chapter you need to be at a certain level to even have a chance. Which means you will keep fighting the same few character to level up and use the same tactic over and over which will turn into quite a chore quickly.
The other major issue is the simplicity of the game. Basically you just use every topic with every character or interaction point until you get the next one. For a game about words, there is disappointingly little choice of dialogue. Or more frankly: none at all. Get key topic, here monologues, get new topic, here monologues, get final topic, manage your meters.

On the bright site, the game is well written, the unfolding story is rather interesting and the game is short enough not to outstay its mechanics' welcome. While it is very linear and the map quite small it still offers enough to explore and find to warrant straying from the direct path.

An nice little game but certainly not everyone's cup of tea.
